title: ‘Build AI at home’: Nvidia strikes Australian deals
full_text:
The $US5 trillion ($6.93 trillion) artificial-intelligence juggernaut Nvidia has signed deals with top data centre operators including Firmus and AirTrunk for 2 gigawatts of capacity by 2027, marking a major Australian investment for the world’s most valuable company.
As foreshadowed by The Australian on Monday, Nvidia will collaborate with Firmus, AirTrunk, NextDC, CDC, Sharon AI, Iren, Reset Data and Megaport as it seeks to expand land, power and shell capacity to host multiple generations of its DSX compute infrastructure.
The Jensen Huang-fronted tech giant said providers will operate the AI factories, with Nvidia delivering the DSX platform, accelerated computing, networking, software and ecosystem support.
Delivering 2GW by 2027 underlines the rampant acceleration of the industry in Australia while also raising questions over whether the national power grid can deliver enough renewable energy to meet demand.
Transgrid commissioned its own modelling on data centres’ giant thirst for electricity supplies that shows demand at double the level of a widely used forecast from the power grid operator, underlining the uncertain energy needs of the booming AI factories.
The deal follows Labor figures Richard Marles and Andrew Charlton personally delivering Labor’s pitch for the booming industry last week in the US.
A delegation led by the Deputy Prime Minister and Assistant Technology Minister to attract AI infrastructure investment was received by the world’s biggest tech names, including Mr Huang, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and OpenAI chief Sam Altman.
The Mike Cannon-Brookes-led Atlassian along with Heidi will also build regional AI models, applications and agents for industries nationwide with expanded access to Nvidia’s accelerated computing and Nemotron open models.
Nvidia said expanded capacity will give Australian innovators “greater access to accelerated computing” and Nvidia Nemotron open models to develop locally relevant models, applications and agents, while supporting regional and global demand for AI compute. “Through our partnerships with Australian NCPs, this infrastructure can support multiple generations of Nvidia compute and expand local access to accelerated computing and Nvidia Nemotron open models, helping Australian innovators build AI at home,” said Raj Mirpuri, Nvidia’s vice-president of global AI clouds and infrastructure ecosystem.
Nvidia already has exposure to Australia with an equity stake in the Oliver Curtis-led Firmus Technologies, with the pair signing a new strategic partnership on the back of a $US30bn Indonesian data centre deal in June.
Firmus may now command a $30bn valuation ahead of its initial public offering expected in October, with the Sydney-based company this week landing Mr Altman’s OpenAI as a customer, putting the homegrown tech plater on track for the largest ASX listing this decade.
Nvidia describes DSX as a “full-stack AI factory platform” spanning facilities infrastructure, computing, networking, software and reference designs.
“Australia’s established sustainable energy and digital infrastructure, deep technology talent and reputation as a trusted global economic partner provide a strong foundation for start-ups, universities, researchers, enterprises, developers and AI-native companies to train, deploy and scale AI,” Nvidia said.
Australia is already juggling a $150bn data centre spree but Mr Charlton has said the nation must capitalise on that growth to expand Australia’s AI training ecosystem.
Existing copyright laws require AI companies to secure permission to use Australian creative works, data and other copyrighted content for model training.
While a text and data mining exemption in Australian copyright law has been ruled out, failing to win hundreds of billions of dollars of investment from the world’s most powerful tech companies stands as a major political and economic risk should a deal fail to be hashed out. Anthropic, which is preparing a blockbuster US sharemarket listing by October, would likely commit to a major data centre expansion in Australia should it win approval for Australia to emerge as an additional base for training its Claude model.
